title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
text: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models combine pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for language generation. The retriever uses Dense Passage Retrieval (DPR) over Wikipedia chunks, while the generator is a seq2seq model (BART). RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved document for the whole sequence, whereas RAG-Token can use different documents per token. Experiments show RAG establishes state-of-the-art results on open-domain question answering benchmarks including Natural Questions and TriviaQA while generating more specific and factual language.

title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
text: Self-RAG introduces a framework to train a single language model to dynamically retrieve, generate, and critique text using reflection tokens. The model generates special tokens: [Retrieve] to decide whether to fetch external evidence, [IsRel] to judge passage relevance, [IsSup] to evaluate if the generated text is fully supported by the retrieved passage, and [IsUse] to judge output usefulness. During inference, beam search is guided by the critique tokens to filter unsupported sentences, dramatically reducing factual hallucinations and improving citation precision in open-domain QA and long-form synthesis.

title: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation
text: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (CRAG) addresses the robustness of RAG when retrieved documents contain irrelevant or misleading information. CRAG employs a lightweight retrieval evaluator to assess the quality of retrieved passages, producing a confidence score that triggers three actions: Correct (decompose and filter retrieved text), Incorrect (trigger external web search to rectify knowledge deficiency), or Ambiguous (combine filtered retrieval with web search). This prevents misleading evidence from poisoning generative synthesis.

title: Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT
text: In a comprehensive empirical evaluation of academic citations generated by ChatGPT, the authors found that 47% of generated citations were completely fabricated (non-existent papers, journals, or invalid DOIs). Among the remaining citations referencing real publications, 46% contained substantive metadata errors in author names, publication year, volume numbers, or pagination. Furthermore, when citations accompanied scientific prose, the cited papers frequently did not support the specific claims made by the model.

title: Hallucination Rates and Reference Accuracy of ChatGPT and Bard for Systematic Reviews: Comparative Analysis
text: This study evaluated ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, and Google Bard on reference generation for systematic medical reviews across orthopedic surgery and gynecology. The overall reference hallucination rate was 38% for GPT-4 and 55% for GPT-3.5. Only 22% of generated references were completely accurate in both bibliographic existence and claim support. The study warns that conversational LLMs cannot be relied upon for academic reference lists without independent librarian or human verification.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
text: This survey organizes RAG paradigms into Naive RAG, Advanced RAG, and Modular RAG. Naive RAG follows a retrieve-then-read strategy which often encounters low precision, low recall, and hallucination during synthesis. Advanced RAG incorporates pre-retrieval optimization (query rewriting, routing) and post-retrieval reranking and context compression. Modular RAG enables flexible routing between search engines, databases, and verification modules.

title: Can large language models replace humans in systematic reviews? Evaluating GPT-4's efficacy in screening and extracting data
text: Khraisha et al. tested GPT-4 across multiple screening and data extraction stages in systematic reviews. GPT-4 achieved high recall (92%) on title-abstract screening but showed poor specificity (36%), resulting in high false inclusion rates. Data extraction accuracy varied dramatically depending on whether prompts were zero-shot or few-shot and whether input tables were cleanly parsed. The authors concluded that LLMs should assist rather than replace human systematic reviewers.

title: Artificial Hallucinations in ChatGPT: Implications in Scientific Writing
text: Alkaissi and McFarlane documented instances of artificial hallucinations where ChatGPT synthesized convincing clinical vignettes and biomedical arguments supported by completely fabricated citations. The fabricated papers had plausible titles, real co-authors mixed with invented ones, and fake PubMed IDs. The authors emphasize that scientific peer reviewers and editors must verify bibliographic records against PubMed and CrossRef databases.

title: Comparing scientific abstracts generated by ChatGPT to real abstracts with detectors and blinded human reviewers
text: Blinded human reviewers and AI output detectors evaluated ChatGPT-generated scientific abstracts based on titles from high-impact medical journals (JAMA, NEJM, BMJ). Human reviewers failed to identify 32% of generated abstracts as artificial, identifying only 68% correctly. However, generated abstracts frequently contained subtle numerical contradictions and hallucinated patient cohort sizes that did not match real medical registries.

title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
text: ReAct combines verbal reasoning traces with interactive actions (e.g. search, lookup, finish) in an external environment such as Wikipedia. Reasoning traces allow the model to track progress, decompose multi-step problems, and formulate search queries, while actions retrieve external observations to update parametric knowledge and ground subsequent thoughts.

title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
text: This comprehensive survey categorizes hallucinations in NLG into intrinsic hallucinations (contradicting source information) and extrinsic hallucinations (adding ungrounded assertions that cannot be verified from the source). In dialogue, summarization, and translation, hallucinations stem from representation learning shortcuts, unconstrained decoding, and knowledge divergence between pre-training corpora and inference tasks.

title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
text: DPR demonstrates that dense retrieval based on dual-encoder BERT architectures outperforms traditional sparse BM25 retrieval by 9-19% in top-20 passage retrieval accuracy. Dual encoders map questions and text passages into a continuous embedding space where maximum inner product search (MIPS) retrieves candidate evidence for downstream reader models.

title: FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long-form Text Generation
text: FActScore introduces a framework for evaluating factual precision in long-form generation by decomposing generated responses into atomic facts (individual claim statements). Each atomic fact is evaluated independently against a verified knowledge source to compute the percentage of supported atomic claims, demonstrating that standard commercial LLMs achieve under 60% factual accuracy on entity biographies.

title: Enabling Large Language Models to Generate Text with Citations
text: The ALCE benchmark evaluates LLMs on generating responses with citations. ALCE measures citation precision (percentage of cited statements supported by references) and citation recall (percentage of statements backed by citations). Standard prompting produces low citation precision (below 50%), and LLMs frequently cite documents as plausible decorations rather than genuine evidence sources.

title: Evaluating Open-Domain Question Answering in the Era of Large Language Models
text: This paper analyzes the evaluation protocols of modern QA systems. It reveals that exact match (EM) metrics penalize valid synonymous answers, while lexical ROUGE scores fail to capture factual contradictions. The authors advocate for reference-grounded token attribution and entailment checking to measure factual consistency.

title: Retrieval Augmentation Reduces Hallucination in Conversation
text: The authors examine dialogue agents and show that integrating neural retrieval with large generative models significantly reduces hallucinated statements from 45% down to under 15%. However, when retrieved passages are only partially relevant, models still suffer from conversational fabrication.

title: Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models
text: Chain-of-Verification (CoVe) enables language models to deliberate on their own outputs by generating verification questions, executing verification independently, and generating a revised, factually consistent response. CoVe yields substantial gains in factual precision across list generation and long-form scientific query answering.

title: Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models
text: Llama 2 introduces open-access models from 7B to 70B parameters. Safety and helpfulness fine-tuning uses Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). Evaluation shows that while chat variants exhibit strong conversational ability, parametric knowledge cutoff boundaries prevent accurate synthesis of post-September 2022 research without retrieval.

title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
text: GPT-3 evaluates 175B parameter autoregressive models on few-shot in-context learning. Scaling law results show significant zero-shot and few-shot capabilities across reasoning and translation, but models exhibit hallucination on factual queries and cannot update internal parameters post-training.

title: Language Models are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
text: Demonstrated that language models trained on WebText can perform downstream tasks in a zero-shot manner without parameter fine-tuning. Identified the fundamental limitation of fixed training sets and parametric memory decay over time.
